summary: Design a cache with O(1) get and put that evicts the least recently used entry when full.
mainInsight: A hash map gives O(1) lookup by key; a doubly linked list orders entries by recency with O(1) insert/removal at known nodes. The map stores key -> node, so touching an entry means unlinking its node and re-inserting it at the head; eviction removes the tail.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Min-heap + hash set of keys: Updating recency in a heap is O(log n) and awkward.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Stack + queue with a counter: Cannot remove from the middle in O(1).

promptVariants: Why must the list be doubly linked and why does the map store nodes rather than values?
cards.answer: To move an accessed entry to the front you must unlink it from the middle, which needs its prev and next pointers (doubly linked) and direct access to the node (the map stores node references). Everything else is pointer rewiring at the head/tail in O(1).
cards.explanation: A singly linked list would need O(n) to find the predecessor.

promptVariants: What invariants hold between the hash map and the list after every operation?
State the consistency conditions of the LRU cache.
cards.answer: The map contains exactly the keys present in the list; list order runs from most recent (after head) to least recent (before tail); the size never exceeds capacity after put returns (eviction removes the tail node and deletes its key from the map).
cards.explanation: Nodes store their key so eviction can delete the map entry.

promptVariants: Time complexity of get and put: ___
Both operations on the hash-map + linked-list LRU run in ___.
cards.explanation: Hash lookups and pointer updates only.

promptVariants: What is the space complexity and what does each entry cost?
What bounds the memory of the LRU cache?
cards.answer: O(capacity): one map entry and one list node per cached item (plus two sentinels).

promptVariants: Why does the node store its key and why is eviction done after inserting?
What do the sentinel head/tail nodes simplify?
cards.answer: When the tail node is removed we only have the node, so it must carry its key to delete the matching map entry. Inserting first then evicting when size exceeds capacity keeps the logic uniform (and works even for capacity 1). Sentinel head/tail nodes mean insert/remove never need special cases for an empty list or the ends.
keyPoints: Node.key needed to delete from the map

cards.explanation: Updating an existing key must also refresh recency but not change the size.
